transcript.text: theres a funny smell from my oven when its on

A funny smell from an oven is usually harmless, but first rule out the one serious cause.

## ⚠️ Safety first: is it a gas oven?
If you smell rotten eggs or sulfur, that may be a gas leak:
• Turn off the oven and don't use any switches, lighters, or flames
• Open windows and doors
• Leave the house and call your gas company's emergency line or emergency services from outside

(Note: a brief faint gas smell for a second or two when a gas oven ignites is normal. A persistent one isn't.)

## Common causes by type of smell

Burning food or smoke
• Spilled food or grease on the oven floor, walls, or heating element
• Fix: Let it cool, then clean it out. Use a baking sheet under dishes that might bubble over.

Chemical or plastic smell
• New oven: Protective coatings and insulation burn off during the first few uses. Run it empty at high heat (about 200–250°C / 400–500°F) for 30–60 minutes with windows open.
• Leftover cleaner: Oven cleaner that wasn't fully wiped off. Wipe the inside with water and run the oven empty.
• Something plastic: A utensil, packaging, or a pan handle may have melted inside or on the element. Check carefully once it's cool.

Electrical or burning-wire smell (electric ovens)
• Could be a failing heating element, wiring, or a fan motor
• Turn it off and stop using it. Signs of a bad element include visible blisters, cracks, or sparking. Have it checked by a technician.

Musty or "dusty" smell
• Common if the oven hasn't been used in a while, or after the self-clean cycle
• Usually fades after one or two uses

## Quick checklist
1. Let it cool and look inside, including the floor, the elements, the drawer underneath, and behind the racks
2. Clean any residue
3. Run it empty for 20–30 minutes with ventilation
4. If the smell persists or seems electrical or gassy, call a professional

Can you tell me more? Is it gas or electric, how new is it, and what does the smell remind you of (burning, chemical, gas, electrical)? That would help narrow it down.
its electric, belling, about 12 years old. smells like hot plastic or something electrical, seems to come from behind the cooker not inside the oven

An electrical or hot plastic smell from behind an electric cooker is something to act on now. The most likely cause is an overheating electrical connection, which is a fire risk.

## Do this now
1. Turn the cooker off at the wall. Use the cooker isolator switch, the large switch (often red) on the wall near the cooker. Ideally also switch off the cooker's circuit breaker at the fuse box (consumer unit), usually labelled "cooker."
2. Don't use it again until it's been checked. That includes the hob, since it shares the same supply.
3. If you see smoke, sparks, or flames, don't use water. Get everyone out and call 999.

## Likely causes
The back of the cooker is where the electrics are, so the usual suspects are:

• The terminal block. This is where the mains cable connects to the cooker, behind a small cover on the back. After years of heating and cooling, the screws can work loose. A loose connection overheats and melts the plastic block. This is very common on older cookers and fits your description well.
• The cooker outlet on the wall. The connection plate behind the cooker, or the isolator switch itself, can overheat for the same reason. Check whether the isolator switch or its faceplate feels warm or looks discoloured.
• The supply cable. It can be damaged, crushed, or touching a hot part of the cooker.
• Internal wiring or the fan motor. On a fan oven, wiring near the rear fan and element can degrade with age.
• Less likely: something fallen down the back, like a plastic bag or utensil, resting against a hot panel.

## What to check, with power off at the fuse box
• Look at the wall outlet and isolator for scorch marks, brown or black discolouration, or melted plastic.
• If you can safely pull the cooker out, check the cable and the back panel for the same signs, and for anything that's fallen behind. Cookers are heavy and often on a short cable, so don't yank it. Get help if needed.

Don't open the terminal cover or any panels yourself unless you're competent with electrics.

## Who to call
• An electrician if the problem looks like it's at the wall outlet or cable.
• An appliance repair engineer for faults inside the cooker. A terminal block replacement is usually a quick, inexpensive job, so the cooker may well be worth fixing even at 12 years old.

A melted connection won't fix itself and tends to get worse, so please don't keep using it in the meantime. It's also worth checking that your smoke alarm is working.

the switch on the wall looks a bit brown at one corner and felt warm when i touched it. i cant pull the cooker out, its too heavy to move on my own. the lights flickered once too and i heard a crackle from the back once

These are signs of an electrical fault that could start a fire. A browned, warm switch plus crackling and flickering lights points to arcing, where electricity jumps across a loose or damaged connection. Act now.

## Do this immediately
1. Switch off the cooker circuit at the fuse box (consumer unit). Flip the breaker labelled "cooker" to off. Don't touch the brown wall switch again, since it's damaged and could be live or hot.
2. If you can't find the right breaker, or the lights flicker again afterwards, switch off the main switch on the consumer unit. That cuts power to the whole house.
3. Call an electrician today. Say you have a scorched, warm cooker isolator with crackling and flickering lights, and ask for an emergency or same-day callout.

## Call 999 if
• You see smoke, sparks or flames, or the burning smell gets stronger
• The switch or wall gets hot even with the power off

If there's a fire, get everyone out, close doors behind you, and don't use water on it.

## While you wait
• Leave the power off. Don't test it to see if it's still happening.
• Make sure your smoke alarms work.
• Avoid using other high-power appliances if you've had to leave the main power on.
• If the flickering affects the whole house or neighbours too, call 105 (the UK power network emergency line). It could be a supply problem.

## What the electrician will likely do
They'll probably replace the cooker isolator and check the wall outlet, the cable, and the terminal block on the back of the cooker. They can also pull the cooker out safely. A replacement isolator is a common, fairly quick job.

Have you managed to switch off the breaker?
